cells.tense: You are reading the structure now, while it is still standing and holding.
cells.ask: Pick one thing you built that people treat as finished, and say out loud what it was for. Then stop at that sentence.
cells.core: You can see the shape of what you've made without needing it in your hands. A plan, a habit, something you set running — you know what holds it up and how far it reaches, and you're not asking anyone to agree with you about it. That's a real kind of knowing, and it doesn't come cheap.\n\nWhat's working is that the pattern doesn't become the story. You're not protecting it and you're not decorating it. It just stands there and you can walk around it. The next thing this is free to feed is the part that holds under pressure, because a thing that's actually finished will get leaned on. Keep your account of it plain. Take the credit that's yours and leave the rest.
cells.sheetLine: You see the shape of what you built, and you don't need it praised.
cells.verb: Building something that outlasts the effort that made it

cells.tense: You will have proof of it working, and you are already rehearsing the ending.
cells.ask: Name the finished thing you keep wanting to show people, and let one week pass without bringing it up.
cells.core: You're reading the shape so hard you're reading the future into it. A pattern was supposed to be seen and released, and instead you're running it forward, testing it against endings that haven't happened, treating a conversation as a chance to show the structure is sound. The proof is doing work the thing already does.\n\nWhat gets lost is the daily feel of it. You know how it works and you've stopped noticing that it does. The direction is genuine — it just arrived before its moment and started speaking for it. The way back is to be open to what's actually in front of you and let it be smaller than the pattern. One piece of it, today, as it is rather than as evidence.

cells.tense: You stopped looking at it, and the thing you built sits back there now.
cells.ask: Look at one thing you finished and set down. Say what it's doing now, in plain words, and leave it there.
cells.core: Seeing how a thing holds together went quiet. Where there used to be a clear account of it, there's a gap — so you wait for someone to tell you what you have, or you don't look at all. Not because the thing isn't there. Because when you last looked, it didn't go the way you wanted, and you haven't been back since.\n\nThis isn't a sight problem. It's charge. You can't read a pattern when there's nothing in the tank, and pushing attention into a starved place only makes the starvation clearer. What helps is doing the small expressive act first — making something, saying something, without checking whether it's good — and letting your sight come back on its own.

cells.tense: You are already reading the structure, and you talk about it as if it read itself.
cells.ask: Take one thing you describe as having worked out on its own, and say instead that you saw it through. Out loud, once.
cells.core: You walk into a situation and you see the mechanism, the load paths, what holds and what won't — faster than you can account for. Then you say the thing worked itself out, or the timing was right, or it was obvious once you looked. Reading it happened. Telling anyone it was yours didn't.\n\nThat's not modesty. Modesty would let you keep the fact and just lower the tone. What's happening is the pattern gets treated as something that arrived on its own, and the one who read it drops out of the sentence. You don't need a bigger story about it. You need the plain one. This is your reading, and it belongs to whoever did it.
